newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada union pressing GM to accept pattern deal.
newsitem.headline: Canada union pressing GM to accept pattern deal.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers union (CAW) said on Monday it will break off its sub-committee and local talks with the Canadian subsidiary of General Motors Corp. if the automaker does not accept the key terms forged by the union in its deal with Chrysler Corp..

"If we are not successful at getting a breakthrough on the key issues by our caucus meeting at five o'clock (5 p.m. EDT/2100 GMT) today we will call off all meetings that are scheduled this evening," CAW President Buzz Hargrove told reporters at a morning press briefing.
Hargrove said he would continue to bargain with GM at the master table, providing the talks focused exclusively on outsourcing and a pattern agreement.

GM Canada's lead negotiator, Dean Munger, said he would prefer the union not break off talks at the lower levels because it would make it difficult to conclude an agreement on all issues before Wednesday's midnight strike deadline.

"I'd just soon not have him (Hargrove) do that and we're going to work together to try to resolve our issues so that doesn't happen," Munger said. "We believe that we can still achieve a settlement without a strike."

The union chose G.M. Canada one week ago as its second negotiating target after reaching agreement with Chrysler Canada earlier this month. The Chrysler pact, ratified last weekend, halts plant sales and closings during the three-year agreement and commits Chrysler to replace any union jobs lost due to work done by outside contractors, known as outsourcing.

At the heart of the disagreement is the CAW's determination to apply the Chrysler deal on outsourcing, which would reverse G.M. Canada's intentions to sell two plants and contract out about 5,500 union jobs.
"Before we leave the bargaining table we are going to have the Chrysler pattern on outsourcing language," Hargrove said.

By Monday, talks had endured a bomb threat at one of GM's plants, a secret buyer for two Canadian plants, a letter on outsourcing to employees from GM Canada's president and an argument from the union that GM Canada has already shed nearly as many jobs in the last 10 years as exist in total at Ford Motor Co.'s Canadian unit.

Hargove said the union has approved an escalating strike strategy that would close down G.M. operations in Oshawa and St. Therese, Quebec. He said members will walk out of GM's St. Catharines plant on Oct. 6 and close down remaining plants in London and Windsor, Ontario, on Oct. 9.

Neither the company nor the union would speculate on the cost of a strike. But analysts said last week that a strike could cost GM as much as $150 million a week, halt production of some vehicle models and interrupt its U.S. operations.

"A long strike might get to the point where it would be reducing GM's profits by maybe $100 million to $150 million a week," said David Healy, analyst at Burnham Securities Inc. "It could spread south of the (Canada/U.S.) border as well."
However, the United Auto Workers union, which reached a tentative agreement with Chrysler and has ratified a deal with Ford, must now turn to GM in the next couple of weeks.

Hargrove admitted that a UAW strike deadline at GM in the United States would effectively put a halt to Canadian bargaining, but said he had assurances from UAW President Stephen Yokich that would not happen.
"He assured me that will not happen," Hargrove said. "He will not do anything that will interfere with our bargaining."

Earlier this year United Auto Workers union members at a Dayton, Ohio, brake plant walked off the job over outsourcing. The strike lasted 17 days, shut virtually all GM's North American operations and cost the carmaker about $900 million over 17 days.

The CAW's $36.7 million strike fund may make it tough to carry out a long-term strike and pay strike benefits to 28,000 members at GM. But Hargrove said last week that the union had called a special strike dues convention for the entire 210,000-member union on Oct. 18 as a contingency.
